body.hook: Two people can look at the same painting and see completely different things. A critique isn't about saying "I like it" or "I don't." It's a step-by-step way of looking that lets you back up what you think with what you see.

study.title: Four Steps to Seeing
study.question: How can we look closely at art from any culture and respond with evidence?
study.passage:
Choose three artworks from different cultures and times, for example: a Haida bentwood box or button blanket, Katsushika Hokusai's "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" (Japan, about 1831), and a work by a contemporary Canadian artist.
Step 1, Describe (What do I see?): List subject, colours, lines, shapes, textures, medium and size. No opinions yet.
Step 2, Analyze (How is it organized?): Which elements and principles stand out? Where is the focal point? How does the eye move? How is balance or rhythm created?
Step 3, Interpret (What does it mean?): What mood or message does it suggest? What symbols appear? What does the context (culture, time, purpose) add? Use "I think ... because I see ..."
Step 4, Judge (Is it successful?): Decide whether the work succeeds and by which criteria: skill, expression, originality or function.
Respect: When looking at Indigenous and other cultural works, learn what the work means to the culture that made it, use the correct names, and remember that some objects are ceremonial, not decorative.
study.source: Original critique activity written for this lesson using the Feldman four-step model.

study.title: Art Across the World
study.question: How do culture and purpose shape the way art looks?
study.passage:
Three works to compare (teacher shows images):
1. A Haida or Kwakwaka'wakw transformation mask (Northwest Coast, Canada): formline design, bold red and black, made for ceremony and storytelling; opens to reveal another being. Owned and used by families with rights to the stories.
2. Katsushika Hokusai, "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" (Japan, about 1831): woodblock print made in thousands of copies for ordinary people; flat areas of colour, strong outlines, Prussian blue (a newly imported pigment).
3. Leonardo da Vinci, "Mona Lisa" (Italy, about 1503–1519): oil portrait, smooth blending (sfumato), realistic perspective, made for a wealthy patron.
Part 1 (15 minutes): Fill the organizer for each work: purpose, materials, use of line, colour, space and who it was for.
Part 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, write three similarities and three differences between two of the works.
Part 3 (10 minutes): Discuss: Why might a museum display a ceremonial mask differently from a painting? What should viewers know?

body.objective: Students will be able to write a critical response.
body.iCan: I can write a critical response.
successCriteria: I can plan a critical response with a clear claim
I can support my interpretation with visual evidence and context
I can write in a formal, respectful voice
body.hook: Art critics, gallery labels and university essays all do the same thing: turn looking into clear writing. A critical response isn't a list of likes and dislikes. It's an argument about an artwork, supported with evidence you can point to.

vocabulary.definition: Writing that analyzes and interprets an artwork and makes a supported judgment.
The main claim of a piece of writing.
Specific details in an artwork that support a point.
Discussion of the elements and principles of design.
Specific terms such as contrast, composition and texture.

study.title: Writing About Art
study.question: How do I write a clear, supported critical response?
study.passage:
Structure (five paragraphs, 400–500 words):
1. Introduction: title, artist, date, medium, one sentence of context, and a thesis. Example: "In 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa,' Hokusai uses contrast in scale and dynamic line to show the power of nature over human life."
2. Description: what is shown, without opinion.
3. Formal analysis: two or three elements or principles with specific visual evidence ("the claw-like foam at the crest," "the tiny Mount Fuji framed by the wave").
4. Interpretation: meaning, supported by evidence and context (Japan's relationship with nature, the popularity of prints).
5. Judgment and conclusion: is the work successful? By what criteria? Restate the thesis in new words.
Style: present tense, formal voice (no "I think it's cool"), art vocabulary, quotes of short labels or titles only.
Activity: Read a weak paragraph ("This painting is really nice and the colours are good") and a strong one; list what makes the strong one better. Then plan your own response with the organizer and draft the thesis and analysis paragraph.
